children.title: Photosynthesis & Cellular Respiration
children.description: How plants bottle sunlight as sugar and how every cell cashes that sugar in for usable energy — the two reactions that run all of life.

children.title: Photosynthesis: Inputs & Outputs
children.description: What goes into photosynthesis, what comes out, and where it happens.

teach.headline: Sunlight In, Sugar and Oxygen Out
teach.body:
Photosynthesis runs inside the **chloroplast**. It takes in **carbon dioxide, water, and light energy** and puts out **glucose** (a sugar) and **oxygen**:

6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂

Worth sitting with: the oxygen in the breath you just took, and the sugar in whatever you last ate, both came out of this one reaction happening in leaves.

![Chloroplast diagram showing thylakoids and stroma where photosynthesis occurs](/content/bio-eoc/figures/bio_eoc_chloroplast.svg)

figures.alt: Cross-section of a chloroplast with outer membrane, thylakoid stacks, and stroma labeled
figures.caption: Photosynthesis occurs inside the chloroplast.

teach.mnemonic: IN: CO2 + WATER + LIGHT. OUT: GLUCOSE + OXYGEN. The chloroplast bottles sunlight as sugar.
teach.poweredIdea: Photosynthesis uses CO2, water, and light to make glucose and oxygen inside the chloroplast.

data.scenario: A student places a sprig of an aquatic plant in water under a bright lamp. Within minutes, small gas bubbles rise from the plant.

data.runNarrative: Bright light drives photosynthesis. The plant uses carbon dioxide and water to build glucose and releases oxygen as a product. That oxygen comes out of solution as visible bubbles.
data.truthSummary: Bubbles from a brightly lit aquatic plant are oxygen — a product of photosynthesis.

bugCandidates.explanation: The lamp's warmth is not boiling the water; the gas is a product of photosynthesis.

children.title: Light Energy to Chemical Energy
children.description: How captured sunlight becomes the chemical energy that feeds food chains.

teach.headline: Sunlight Becomes Energy You Can Eat
teach.body:
**Chlorophyll** inside the chloroplast absorbs light. Photosynthesis then converts that **light (solar) energy into chemical energy** locked in the bonds of **glucose**.

Plants are **producers**: they bottle the Sun's energy as sugar, and almost every food chain on Earth runs on that stored sunlight. The calories in your breakfast are, very literally, repackaged sunshine.
teach.mnemonic: PHOTO = LIGHT. Chlorophyll catches LIGHT and locks it into SUGAR bonds — edible sunshine.
teach.poweredIdea: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy stored in the bonds of glucose.

data.prompt: Photosynthesis converts light energy into _____ energy stored in glucose.

data.explanation: Producers convert sunlight into chemical energy in glucose, and that stored energy flows up the chain.

achievement.flavor: You follow sunlight into sugar bonds and see why producers feed nearly every food chain on Earth.

children.title: Cellular Respiration: Inputs & Outputs
children.description: What cells feed into respiration to make the ATP that powers everything they do.

teach.headline: Burning Sugar to Make ATP
teach.body:
Cellular respiration happens mainly in the **mitochondria**. It takes in **glucose and oxygen** and puts out **carbon dioxide, water, and ATP** (the energy currency cells actually spend):

C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + ATP

Every heartbeat, every muscle twitch, every thought you're having right now is paid for in ATP made by this reaction.
teach.mnemonic: IN: GLUCOSE + OXYGEN. OUT: CO2 + WATER + ATP. Mitochondria cash sugar in for usable energy.
teach.poweredIdea: Cellular respiration breaks glucose with oxygen in the mitochondria to make CO2, water, and ATP.

children.title: Aerobic vs Fermentation
children.description: Why oxygen makes the difference between a big ATP payout and a small one.

teach.headline: With Oxygen vs Without It
teach.body:
With oxygen, **aerobic** respiration fully breaks down glucose and yields a large amount of ATP — about **36** per glucose. When oxygen runs low, cells switch to **fermentation** (anaerobic), which yields only about **2** ATP and leaves behind lactic acid (in muscle) or alcohol and CO₂ (in yeast).

That burn in your legs at the end of a hard sprint is fermentation: your muscles outran their oxygen supply and dropped to the low-yield backup.
teach.mnemonic: OXYGEN = JACKPOT (~36 ATP). NO OXYGEN = FERMENT, scrape ~2 ATP + lactic acid — hence the burn.
teach.poweredIdea: Aerobic respiration yields far more ATP than anaerobic fermentation, the low-oxygen backup.

data.story: During an all-out sprint, a runner's leg muscles start to burn and build up lactic acid.
data.question: What best explains this?
data.answer: Oxygen can't be delivered fast enough, so the muscles switch to fermentation.

The muscles stopped making ATP entirely.
Extra oxygen flooded the muscles and caused the burn.
data.explanation: Intense effort outpaces oxygen delivery, so muscles use anaerobic fermentation, which produces lactic acid.

data.story: Yeast cells ferment glucose when oxygen is limited, as in bread dough rising or wine production.
data.question: What are the main products of yeast fermentation, and how does ATP yield compare to aerobic respiration?
data.answer: Alcohol and CO₂ with about 2 ATP — far less than aerobic respiration (~36 ATP).
options: Alcohol and CO₂ with about 2 ATP — far less than aerobic respiration (~36 ATP).
Lactic acid and O₂ with about 36 ATP — the same as aerobic respiration.
Glucose and water with about 2 ATP — more than aerobic respiration.
Alcohol and CO₂ with about 36 ATP — more than aerobic respiration.
data.explanation: Yeast fermentation yields alcohol and carbon dioxide plus only about 2 ATP per glucose — aerobic respiration extracts far more energy.

children.title: Photosynthesis & Respiration Loop
children.description: How the two reactions mirror each other — and why plants run both.

teach.headline: Two Halves of One Energy Loop
teach.body:
Photosynthesis and cellular respiration are mirror images. Photosynthesis **stores** solar energy in glucose and releases O₂; respiration **releases** that energy from glucose to make ATP and gives off CO₂. The products of one are the reactants of the other.

Key point students miss: **plants do both.** A plant makes glucose by photosynthesis and then runs cellular respiration to use it. You and a maple tree are two ends of the same loop — each breathing out what the other breathes in.
teach.mnemonic: PHOTO STORES, RESPIRATION SPENDS. O2 ↔ CO2, glucose ↔ ATP. PLANTS DO BOTH, not just photo.
teach.poweredIdea: Photosynthesis stores solar energy in glucose; respiration releases it as ATP — and plants do both.

data.hint: How does a plant get usable energy out of the glucose it makes?
data.canonicalFix: Plants run cellular respiration too. They make glucose by photosynthesis and then break it down through respiration to power their own cells.
data.poweredIdea: Plants do both: photosynthesis to store energy and respiration to release it.

data.story: A plant cell has just produced glucose through photosynthesis.
data.question: Which process uses that glucose to make ATP the cell can spend?
data.explanation: Respiration breaks down the glucose made in photosynthesis to release usable energy as ATP.

achievement.flavor: You close the loop: one reaction's products feed the other, and plants run both ends.
